narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 88.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, the admissions decision treated that high risk estimate as the reason to reject your application, even though it is a prediction rather than a certainty. The estimate was based on academic factors; gender and race were not used.

The strongest factor pushing toward failure was your third-year class rank. Your class-rank decile was 1, well below the accepted-student average near 6, and this was the single most influential signal. Your first-year class rank, also 1 against an accepted average near 6, was the second-strongest factor and likewise pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90, below the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor; in the model’s overall balance, it modestly pushed toward passing rather than failing.

To improve your next application, focus on the academic indicators that carried the most weight. Work with an advisor to raise your class rank through strong recent coursework, document any circumstances that affected your early grades, and consider whether retaking the LSAT is realistic given your score of 29 compared with the accepted average of 37.18. Reapply once you can show stronger, more recent evidence of bar-exam readiness.
